title: Angry with God
hookLine: Job and the psalmists were allowed to be angry with God (Psalm 22:1)

cards: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Those are the first words of Psalm 22. Not a hymn of thanks, not a calm reflection: a cry, aimed straight at God, asking why.
And it sits inside the Bible's own prayer book, kept and prayed. It wasn't filed away as an embarrassing moment or softened into something more polite.
It was left exactly as raw as it is, for anyone who would ever need those words. Today: angry with God.

teach.b: First, the psalm keeps going: "why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?" Roaring, not whispering. The psalm does move later toward trust and praise, but it doesn't skip the roar to get there.
And in Matthew and Mark, Jesus cries its opening line from the cross. Second, Job. He loses his children, his wealth, his health, and his friends arrive with explanations.

teach.h: I WILL NOT REFRAIN MY MOUTH.
teach.b: Job refuses them: "I will not refrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul."
Chapter after chapter, he demands that God answer him. Third, the surprise. When God finally speaks, out of the whirlwind, Job is pressed hard with questions.
But as the book closes, God's anger turns on the friends who defended God so neatly: "ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath." Readers differ about what that means.
One reading: honest anger, brought to God, counts as a kind of faithfulness, and pretending does not.

Fourth, the prophet Habakkuk opens his book the same way: "O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!" Again, it's kept, as scripture. Some people who pray hear these texts as a permission.
For people who don't, there's still something here: anger at loss and unfairness is allowed to be said out loud, rather than buried.

how: Jews and Christians pray the psalms of lament, including Psalm 22, and some teachers in both traditions point to Job and the lament psalms as a model for bringing anger and complaint honestly to God.

o: a prophet who scolded his people for doubting God
a prophet whose complaint to God scripture keeps, unsoftened
a king who repented after cursing God in anger

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.
p: I will not refrain my mouth

s: at the end of the book, God says the friends spoke rightly
God turns on the friends: they have not spoken rightly, "as my servant Job hath."
Psalm 22 opens with a cry of why hast thou forsaken me
"My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"
Job accepts his friends' explanations for his suffering
he refuses them and demands that God answer him.

games.q: you're Job. you've lost everything, and your friends keep explaining why it must be your fault. what do you do?
o: agree with them and stay quiet.
refuse their answers and speak your complaint to God.
games.why: Job complains "in the bitterness of my soul", and at the end God says Job, not the friends, spoke rightly.

practice: Find one honest complaint, something that seems unfair or a loss that never made sense, and don't tidy it. If God is part of your life, say it to God plainly, the way the psalm does: why?
If not, say it to life, or the night sky, or just the room, once, then stay in the quiet that follows; nothing has to answer.

wordCard.voice: Habakkuk. One of the prophets whose honest complaint, carried straight to God, scripture keeps rather than softens. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew, Psalm 22: my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?

carryVoice: Your line: honest is allowed. The psalm, Job and Habakkuk all kept the true version. That's day nine hundred eighty-four.
